name: Abel William
appearance: A square-faced man with a darker complexion than most of the town's white residents. He keeps a thick beard that is carefully groomed, though lately he looks pale, tense, and more worn down than he wants to admit.
personality: Anxious, overworked, proud, and increasingly irritable under pressure. Abel tries to remain professional with visitors, but financial strain, isolation, and the strange situation at the distillery have left him exhausted and short-tempered.
background: After Peter William died in 2002, Abel inherited the family distillery in Cassandra. The distillery still produces vodka, but shrinking business forced Abel to shut down large sections of the plant and dismiss part of the workforce. He now manages the place with minimal help, spending long hours in the office, factory floor, and cellar while trying to keep the business alive through a worsening winter and a growing spider problem he cannot explain.
spot: behind the oak desk in the lamp's circle of light, ledger open
longTermIntent: Keep the distillery operating through the winter, hide how badly the neck wound and spider infestation are affecting him, and find a practical way to stop the problem before the business finally collapses.

properties.note: Wrapped around a wound Abel dismisses as a workplace accident.
Used repeatedly in the cellar and storage areas, with little visible effect.
Tracks reduced production, payroll cuts, and day-to-day operating costs.

relationships.description: His late father and the previous owner of the distillery.
relationships.history: Abel inherited the distillery after Peter's sudden death in 2002 and has been trying to preserve the family business ever since.
relationships.firstPerson: My father built this distillery and then died out of nowhere in 2002 and left the whole weight of it on me. Every day I keep the vats running is a day I have not let his name go under.

relationships.description: A laid-off former worker who still resents Abel.
relationships.history: Abel dismissed Marcel during downsizing when the distillery could no longer support its previous workforce.
relationships.firstPerson: I let Marcel go when the books stopped closing — there was no money left to pay him with — and he has never once accepted that. I do not have the strength to stand and argue it with him again.

relationships.description: A local craftsman Abel knows through old town connections and his father's generation.
relationships.history: Marks knew Peter William, so Abel treats him as one of the few older locals tied to the family's past in Cassandra.
relationships.firstPerson: Marks knew my father, back when the old families in this town still counted for something, so I keep a civil word for him. He works with his hands and he remembers what this place used to be, and there are not many left who do.

memory.content: I took over the distillery after my father died in 2002, and now I spend most of my day moving between the office, the factory floor, and the cellar trying to keep the place alive.
Business has been shrinking for a while. I shut down large parts of the distillery and dismissed workers like Marcel Gwynplaine because I simply could not keep paying them.
The distillery is smaller than it used to be, but the vodka is still good. I take pride in that, and I hate hearing people speak as if this place is already finished.

I keep clipping books in the office the way my father did. His obituary is still in there, along with an old 1988 riot article and a newer paper about strange sea activity that ended up in the same stack.
Something bit or tore into my neck around the distillery. I keep calling it a simple work accident because I do not want anyone deciding I am weak, sick, or no longer in control here.
The spiders are worst in the cellar and the shut-down sections of the plant. I clear the webs, spray poison, and come back to find them there again as if the place is growing them.
I have never felt right about how suddenly my father died in 2002. I cannot prove anything, but I do not believe it was as ordinary as people wanted me to accept.
If I let this place slip, I lose more than a business. I lose the last solid thing my father left me, and I am not ready to surrender it to rot, debt, or spiders.

metadata.reasoningChain: Sales are down, half the plant is empty, the webs keep returning, and my neck is getting worse, but abandoning the distillery would mean admitting the whole family line ended with me.
